engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Time Management
chess.body: Chess is a timed game. Use 70-80% of your clock in complex positions, blitz transitions and endgames you know. Common mistake: spending 15 minutes in the opening, then rushing in the critical middlegame. Rule: if a position is complicated and you see candidate moves, spend the time here — not in simple positions. Clock is a resource, not just a constraint.

wisdom.title: Rest is Productive
wisdom.body: High performers rest. Sleep is not laziness — it's when the brain consolidates learning, the body repairs, emotional regulation resets. Cutting sleep to work more is borrowing from tomorrow's performance to pay today's anxiety. Protect 7 hours. It will make you a better analyst, better father, better human.

book.book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
book.author: Ben Horowitz
book.lesson: Horowitz's most cited framework: peacetime CEOs follow rules, build consensus, develop people. Wartime CEOs break rules, make unilateral calls, prioritise survival. The same leadership style that builds a great culture in a period of growth will lose the company in a crisis. The mistake most leaders make: being a peacetime CEO in wartime. When the company is burning — cash running out, key customer leaving, competitor eating your lunch — you cannot run consensus meetings. You need to make fast, clear decisions, even imperfect ones, and demand execution. Know which mode you're in.
book.key_quote: Leadership style must match the situation. A peacetime approach in wartime is as dangerous as a wartime approach in peacetime.
book.action: What mode is your current situation in — peacetime (optimise) or wartime (survive)? Is your leadership style calibrated to it?
crux: There is no recipe for the hard things. Every playbook assumes conditions you won't have.
The Struggle is the default state of building something hard, not evidence of failure.
Wartime and peacetime CEOs are different jobs requiring different behaviour.
Take care of the people, the products, and the profits — in that order.
Tell it like it is. People can handle bad news; they cannot handle being managed.
Train your people. Neglecting it is the most common and most expensive omission.
Hire for strength, not absence of weakness. Every strong person has visible flaws.
Management debt, like technical debt, accrues interest: two people in one job, no performance process, unclear ownership.
Titles and promotions need a defined process or politics fills the vacuum.
One-on-ones belong to the employee. Silence there means information is not reaching you.
Minimise politics by designing systems, not by asking people to be less political.
The struggle is where greatness comes from. Courage is a habit built by making hard calls.
Focus on the battlefield you're on, not the one you wish you were on.
learnings: Nobody's plan survives. The skill is deciding well without enough information.
Transparency scales trust; managed messaging destroys it.
Management debt compounds faster and quieter than technical debt.
Your psychology is the bottleneck more often than the business is.
examples: Loudcloud IPO'd in 2001 into a collapsing market because the private markets were shut — a bad option chosen over a fatal one.
Horowitz sold the managed-services business and pivoted to Opsware with $60m left, telling employees the truth about the odds.
Opsware sold to HP for $1.6bn after multiple near-death moments — none of which the plan anticipated.
adapt: Meta restriction is a wartime problem. Recovery work first, growth experiments after.
Say the real number publicly — 50% win rate, not the flattering framing. Trust is the asset.
Management debt in the stack: two entry points writing the same signals with different logic caused the duplicate rows.
The Struggle during the Dubai search is the job, not a sign it isn't working.

minimalism.title: The Box Test
minimalism.body: Pack a category into a box and seal it. If you have not opened it in a month, you do not need what is inside. Most people cannot name the contents a week later.
minimalism.action: Box one category — cables, kitchen gadgets, old chargers. Date the box.

etiquette.title: Say The Difficult Thing Kindly And Once
etiquette.body: Softening it into unrecognisability is not kindness — it guarantees you say it again, worse, later. Direct and warm. Once.

stillness.title: Do One Thing At A Time
stillness.body: The monastic instruction is: when walking, walk; when eating, eat. Multitasking is the belief that attention divides without loss. It does not.
stillness.action: Do the next task with nothing else open.

father.title: Practise object permanence
father.do: Hide a toy under a cloth while she watches, then let her pull it off. Repeat with longer delays.
father.why: Around 7–8 months this clicks. It is also why separation anxiety starts now — she has learned you continue to exist when you leave, but not yet that you come back.

father.title: Respond to the babble
father.do: When she makes a sound, answer as if it were a sentence. Wait. Let her go again.
father.why: Turn-taking is the structure of conversation, learned months before words. The pause is the important part — filling it teaches her that her turn does not matter.

life_wisdom.teaching: Everything that arises passes. Applied properly this cuts both ways — bad quarters end, and so do good ones.
life_wisdom.apply: In a drawdown or a bad week, ask what will be true in six months. Most acute distress is a mis-estimate of duration.

interview_tech.q: How would you use automation or AI in the finance function without losing control?
interview_tech.a: Automate the deterministic and keep judgement human. Good candidates: bank reconciliation matching, invoice coding, intercompany elimination, variance flagging, and first-draft commentary. Bad candidates: provisioning, impairment, anything requiring an assertion to auditors. The control question is auditability — if you cannot explain how the output was produced and reperform it, it is not usable in a statutory process. Keep a human approval step on anything that posts to the ledger.

interview_tech.q: Your auditor raises going concern. How do you respond?
interview_tech.a: Take it seriously and answer with evidence, not reassurance. Provide a cash flow forecast covering at least twelve months from signing, with the assumptions documented and stress cases run; the status of facilities including expiry dates and covenant projections; and board-approved mitigating actions with dates. If there is material uncertainty, the honest route is disclosure rather than argument — an unqualified opinion with a material uncertainty paragraph is survivable; a fight with the auditor that ends in a qualification is not.

interview_soft.q: What questions do you have for us?
interview_soft.a: Never none. Ask things that reveal you are evaluating them: what does the first 12 months look like for whoever takes this; what is the finance function currently not able to answer that the board keeps asking; how is the relationship between finance and the commercial teams today; and why is the role open. The last one is the most informative and the least asked. Avoid salary and benefits at first interview.

interview_soft.q: Describe a situation where you had incomplete information and had to decide anyway.
interview_soft.a: Forecasting and provisioning are full of these. Structure: what you knew, what you could not know in the time available, the cost of waiting, the assumption you took and why, and how you made the assumption visible rather than burying it. The mark of seniority is deciding with 70% of the information and saying explicitly what would change your mind — say that phrase.

cfo_field.q: Learn the lease standard properly. In the Gulf it is not a footnote.
cfo_field.a: IFRS 16 put every store lease on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Two consequences a CFO must be able to say out loud: EBITDA is now flattered, because rent that used to sit in operating costs is split into depreciation and interest; and leverage ratios move even though nothing about the business changed. If your covenant is set on a pre-IFRS-16 basis, know it before the bank asks.

cfo_field.q: Automation without a control map is how a finance function loses its audit trail.
cfo_field.a: Before automating a process, write down: who can initiate, who approves, what the system does without a human, and where the exception report goes. Automation does not remove controls; it moves them from people to configuration, and configuration drifts silently. The question 'what breaks if this runs wrong for a month before anyone notices' is the one that separates a finance automation from a finance incident.
